title: Riemannian Functionals
notes: Open by framing the chapter as a shift from curvature as a tensor to curvature as an energy. The printed span studies how scalar curvature, volume, and curvature norms behave when the metric is varied. The lecture keeps the objects synthetic and visual so students can inspect the variational mechanisms without relying on copied source figures.

title: The Metric Is The Variable
notes: Emphasize that a functional on metrics is not a function on points of the manifold. A single point of the space of metrics is already a whole Riemannian geometry, and a tangent vector there is a symmetric two-tensor. The first mental move is to replace coordinate changes by metric perturbations.

title: Total Scalar Curvature
notes: Present the Einstein-Hilbert integral as the simplest global curvature ledger. Scalar curvature is local, the volume form depends on the same metric, and the integral couples the two. The diagram shows that both the integrand and the measuring device move when the metric is varied.

title: First Variation: Where Ricci Appears
notes: The first variation is the reason Ricci curvature is unavoidable in this chapter. Up to boundary or divergence terms, changing the metric pairs the perturbation with Ricci minus one half scalar curvature times the metric. This is the variational origin of the Einstein tensor.

title: Volume Constraint And Normalization
notes: Explain the role of constraints before naming critical metrics. Without normalization, scaling the metric changes the total scalar curvature in a predictable but unhelpful way. Fixing volume, or using a scale-invariant quotient, turns the Euler-Lagrange equation into a geometric condition.

title: Constant Scalar Curvature
notes: Make clear that constant scalar curvature is weaker than the Einstein condition. Inside a conformal class, the normalized total scalar curvature asks for scalar curvature to become constant. Across all metrics with fixed volume, the stronger Ricci proportional to the metric condition appears.

title: Scalar Curvature Map
notes: Treat the scalar curvature map as a nonlinear differential operator from metrics to functions. Its derivative turns a metric perturbation into a function, so the slide separates the input tensor from the output scalar field. This is the analytic bridge to solvability and obstruction questions.

title: Adjoint Test And Static Obstructions
notes: The adjoint is a diagnostic rather than a decoration. If the adjoint has a nontrivial kernel, then nearby prescribed scalar curvature problems can have hidden compatibility conditions. Students should read the right-hand box as the obstruction detector for the scalar curvature map.

title: Conformal Directions Are A Laboratory
notes: Use conformal changes as the controlled experiment. They preserve angles while changing scale, so the scalar curvature transformation becomes a tractable elliptic equation. The Yamabe-type question is whether each conformal class contains a representative with constant scalar curvature.

title: Einstein Metrics As Critical Points
notes: Now connect the two levels. Constant scalar curvature solves the constrained problem inside conformal classes, while Einstein metrics solve the full fixed-volume variational problem. The slide deliberately draws the Einstein condition as the smaller target inside the larger constant-scalar-curvature target.

title: Quadratic Curvature Energies
notes: The chapter then raises the degree of the energy. Instead of integrating scalar curvature linearly, it studies integrals of squared curvature quantities. These functionals detect different pieces of curvature and lead to different Euler-Lagrange equations.

title: Curvature Decomposition Organizes Energies
notes: Use the decomposition as bookkeeping for the quadratic functionals. The full curvature tensor splits into Weyl, traceless Ricci, and scalar parts, so an L squared energy can emphasize conformal curvature, Einstein defect, or average scalar curvature. This makes the formulas less opaque.

title: Gradient, Hessian, Stability
notes: A functional gives more than an Euler-Lagrange equation. Its gradient tells the direction of steepest change, while the Hessian at a critical metric tests local rigidity or instability. In Einstein geometry, this is where analytic operator theory starts governing moduli behavior.

title: Model Metrics For Sanity Checks
notes: Work through the three model rows as sanity checks. Space forms make every curvature piece constant, flat tori kill all curvature energies, and products can have constant scalar curvature without being Einstein unless the factors are balanced. These examples prevent overreading a single equation.

title: Common Misreadings
notes: Pause on the warning slide because variational language invites false shortcuts. Critical for one functional does not mean critical for every curvature energy, constant scalar curvature does not imply Einstein, and rescaling must be handled before comparing numerical values of integrals.

title: Lecture Recap
notes: Close by turning the lecture into a checklist for the notebook. Identify the variable, choose the normalization, compute the first variation, inspect the scalar curvature map, decompose curvature for quadratic energies, and test the claim on model metrics. That is the working grammar of this source span.
